title: How Lie Detectors Work
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how lie detectors (polygraphs) work, starting with the 1920s Berkeley case of Helen Graham and John Larson, and the early proponents like Leonard Keeler who marketed the device. They cover pre-history (Lombroso, Vittorio Benussi, James Mackenzie, the unigraph), the three measurements (respiration via pneumographs, cardiovascular changes via blood pressure cuff, and galvanic skin response via finger electrodes), the pretest, control and relevant questions, and forensic psychophysiologist training. They discuss scoring subjectivity, false positives and negatives (including Gary Ridgeway), legal admissibility (New Mexico, federal judges), the Employee Polygraph Protection Act, countermeasures, fMRI lie detection, and penile plethysmography. The episode ends with a listener mail segment from Brad with satirical suggestions for the show.

segments.title: Opening banter and early polygraph history in Berkeley
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about the 'you lie' Saturday Night Live skit, then tell the story of the 1920s Berkeley campus theft case in which John Larson used a cardio-pneumo-psychograph on suspect Helen Graham, who confessed. They note William Marston invented the device and Leonard Keeler marketed it.

segments.title: Prehistory of the polygraph
segments.summary: Early devices measuring blood pressure and breathing are described, including Cesare Lombroso, Vittorio Benussi, James Mackenzie's 1906 use of the term polygraph, and the unigraph. The hosts stress that polygraphs measure physiological changes and are not true lie detectors.
topics: polygraph is not a lie detector

segments.title: Components of a polygraph test
segments.summary: The three main measurements are explained: respiration via pneumograph tubes around the chest and abdomen, cardiovascular changes via a blood pressure cuff, and electrodermal activity (galvanic skin response) via finger electrodes measuring sweat-related conductivity. The shift from paper ink-pen readouts to digital transducers is noted.

segments.title: Subjectivity and forensic psychophysiologists
segments.summary: The hosts discuss criticism from the ACLU and others that polygraph data is subjective. They describe the 5,000 to 10,000 US examiners, the lack of licensing in many states, and the Académie training requirements (bachelor's degree or investigative experience, a ten-week course, and twenty-five reviewed exams) described by Kevin Bondser's interview with Bob Lee.

segments.title: How the polygraph test is conducted
segments.summary: The pretest interview is described, in which examiners profile the subject. The hosts explain control questions, relevant questions, and irrelevant questions, and how examiners compare responses to the control baseline to judge deception or inconclusive results.

segments.title: Countermeasures and legal admissibility
segments.summary: Popular countermeasures such as sedatives, antiperspirant, and tacks in the shoe are described. The hosts explain that polygraph results are generally inadmissible in court except in New Mexico, with federal judges deciding case by case.

segments.title: Accuracy problems, employment use, and Gary Ridgeway
segments.summary: False positives and false negatives are defined. Gary Ridgeway, the Green River killer, is cited as passing a polygraph before killing more women. The federal government is described as the largest consumer of polygraph exams, and the Employee Polygraph Protection Act bars most private employers from requiring them.

segments.title: fMRI lie detection and penile plethysmography
segments.summary: The hosts discuss using MRI to detect lies in the brain and its early state and ethical questions. They then describe penile plethysmography used on sex offenders and a study at UGA that used it to test homophobic men's arousal to gay pornography.

segments.title: Closing requests and promotions
segments.summary: Chuck jokes about taking a polygraph in the Atlanta area, and the hosts point listeners to the How Stuff Works site for lie detector animation. They invite listeners to offer polygraph access and promote the video podcast Stuff from the Future and a camera sponsor.

segments.title: Listener mail from Brad
segments.summary: Brad's satirical suggestions for the show are read: nicknames, removing personal anecdotes, a memoir podcast, and layering listener mail over tribal drums and jungle noises.
